methodology.scope: Causal forensic completion for TON, Hedera, Gnosis, Osmosis, and Stacks, plus an immutable corrective prelude for the five profiles introduced by migration 0073.
methodology.observation_rule: Volatile DefiLlama figures for this cohort were fetched in one sequential API run beginning at 2026-08-03T17:23:37.879Z and ending at 2026-08-03T17:23:58.550Z. Currency aggregates are canonicalized to cents. The exact retrieval window and returned values are retained because a provider can revise the latest same-day point. Metrics describe outcomes; they do not prove why an outcome occurred.
methodology.causality_rule: Primary protocol, governance, and operator sources establish documented architecture, choices, and response actions. Independent reporting and independent data test incidents and observed adoption. Operator claims are never promoted as independent proof, and strategic explanations are labeled as inference rather than measurement.
methodology.preservation_rule: Migration 0075 patches forensic_analysis on synthesis rows and review metadata on _meta rows. It preserves all legacy identity, token, capital, onchain, team, narrative, risk, links, and synthesis fields. The corrective prelude updates only the merged 0073 forensic contracts and does not rewrite migration 0073.
methodology.review_rule: All profiles were reviewed on 2026-08-03 and are due for review on 2026-08-10. The stored prose is a dated research judgment, not a claim of real-time freshness.

Currency aggregates were rounded to cents. Same-day historical points can be revised after this retrieval window.

outcome.label: middling
outcome.summary: TON is a high-distribution but middling L1: Telegram access and stablecoin circulation are substantial, while capital depth and reliability remain weaker than the reach implies. In the DefiLlama snapshot begun at 2026-08-03T17:23:37.879Z, the latest 2026-08-03 point was $60.3 million TVL, 92.3% below the July 2024 peak, alongside $790.6 million of dollar stablecoins, $143.3 million of 30-day DEX volume, $27.1 million of fees, and $1.17 million of retained revenue. Two reported outages in August 2024 and the earlier inscription-load incident keep the distribution advantage from supporting a stronger reliability call. These figures are a point-in-time snapshot.

why.summary: Observed: TON carries a stablecoin base far larger than its DeFi TVL and produces material gross fees, yet TVL remains more than ninety percent below peak and retained revenue is a small share of those fees. Documented design: the community continued Telegram's custom asynchronous architecture after Telegram withdrew, then leaned into wallet, mini-app, payment, and digital-asset distribution inside Telegram rather than EVM portability. Strategic inference: that channel can create consumer transactions and stablecoin movement without first building deep DeFi collateral, explaining why conventional TVL understates reach but not proving durable token value capture. The same choices concentrate platform dependency and custom-tooling risk. The 2023 load report and two 2024 outages show that distribution spikes can exceed validator readiness; they test the architecture but do not establish that Telegram integration caused every reliability failure.

strategic_choices.decision: Continue the original TON architecture as a community network after Telegram stopped development.
strategic_choices.consequence: The chain preserved differentiated code and an existing community instead of restarting, but inherited naming, governance, and regulatory-history confusion from the abandoned issuer-led project.

strategic_choices.decision: Use a custom asynchronous, dynamically sharded execution model rather than EVM compatibility.
strategic_choices.consequence: TON can optimize for high-throughput consumer services, while developers, validators, and tooling must handle unfamiliar execution and cross-shard behavior.

strategic_choices.decision: Make Telegram the primary wallet, mini-app, and payment distribution surface.
strategic_choices.consequence: Applications can reach a very large existing audience, but policy, product, and integration decisions outside base-layer governance become systemic dependencies.

strategic_choices.decision: Prioritize rapid consumer launches and open validator participation while addressing capacity limits through software and operator upgrades.
strategic_choices.consequence: Demand can be admitted quickly, but the inscription report and later outages show that slow operator coordination can turn load events into prolonged liveness failures.

counterfactual.summary: An EVM-compatible relaunch might have reduced developer friction and imported more DeFi liquidity, but it would have discarded the custom actor and sharding model and still would not guarantee Telegram distribution. A slower, capacity-gated rollout could have reduced the probability of load-driven stalls, at the cost of limiting the consumer experiments that produced TON's distinct adoption channel. The evidence supports those trade-offs, not a claim that either alternative would have retained more capital or avoided every outage.

watch.signal: Stablecoin supply, DeFi TVL, DEX volume, gross fees, and retained revenue tracked separately.
watch.implication: Broad improvement would show Telegram distribution converting into a deeper economy; stablecoins and fees growing alone would leave capital depth and value capture unresolved.

watch.signal: Public incident reports, block-production interruptions, and validator upgrade participation.
watch.implication: Fewer stalls under comparable demand would support the scaling thesis; repeated coordination failures would keep reliability as the binding constraint.

watch.signal: Material changes to Telegram integration, wallet defaults, or TON Foundation governance.
watch.implication: Deeper integration strengthens distribution but increases correlated platform risk; weaker integration tests whether demand survives without privileged placement.

unknowns.question: How concentrated are validator stake, hosting, and emergency-upgrade coordination today?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A current independent entity-level validator and infrastructure map.

unknowns.question: What contractual or technical commitments govern Telegram's long-term TON distribution?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Public durable integration terms or a documented platform-governance commitment.

unknowns.question: How much stablecoin supply is actively transferred or deployed rather than idle in a small number of accounts?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Independent holder, transfer, and application-concentration analysis.

outcome.label: middling
outcome.summary: Hedera is a functioning enterprise-oriented network with a middling economic outcome. In the DefiLlama snapshot begun at 2026-08-03T17:23:37.879Z, the latest 2026-08-03 point was $24.7 million TVL, 88.5% below the January 2025 peak, alongside $36.6 million of dollar stablecoins, $72.9 million of 30-day DEX volume, $239,075 of fees, and $43,751 of retained revenue. Its identifiable Council and native services provide an accountable operating model, but current consensus admission remains permissioned and the independent capital and revenue observations do not validate broad enterprise adoption. These figures are a point-in-time snapshot.

why.summary: Observed: Hedera retains modest stablecoin, DEX, fee, and revenue activity, while TVL remains almost ninety percent below peak. Documented design: the network chose hashgraph consensus, predictable service pricing, native token and consensus services, EVM compatibility, and governance by a rotating council of named organizations. It later moved the open-source codebase into Linux Foundation Decentralized Trust, but its own FAQ still describes live consensus nodes as permissioned. Strategic inference: identifiable operators and specialized services can lower procurement and operational friction for enterprise workloads, while the same admission model narrows permissionless credibility and does not automatically create composable liquidity. The 2023 precompile exploit and the decision to disable proxies demonstrate fast coordinated response and concentrated intervention power at the same time. Neither operator transaction claims nor Council membership is treated here as independent proof of durable fee-paying demand.

strategic_choices.decision: Govern the network through a term-limited council of identifiable global organizations.
strategic_choices.consequence: Members provide accountability and operational coordination, but governance and consensus admission remain concentrated relative to permissionless validator systems.

strategic_choices.decision: Offer native consensus and token services alongside EVM smart contracts.
strategic_choices.consequence: Some enterprise workloads can avoid contract overhead, while developers and auditors must reason about interactions between native services, precompiles, and EVM applications.

strategic_choices.decision: Donate the core codebase to Linux Foundation Decentralized Trust as Project Hiero.
strategic_choices.consequence: Development governance becomes more open and vendor-neutral, but code governance alone does not make live consensus-node admission permissionless.

strategic_choices.decision: Use coordinated network controls during the 2023 precompile exploit.
strategic_choices.consequence: Operators contained further access while patching the defect, showing response capacity and the practical power of a small known operator set.

counterfactual.summary: Opening consensus-node admission earlier could have improved neutrality and reduced the gap between open-source branding and live participation, but it would have weakened the Council's direct control over operator quality and incident coordination. Building only EVM contracts on an existing chain would have avoided a new consensus and governance system, but also surrendered native ordered-consensus and token-service differentiation. The reviewed evidence does not show that either alternative would have produced more enterprise revenue or prevented the precompile defect.

watch.signal: Permissionless-node milestones and the actual composition of consensus operators.
watch.implication: Open admission with diversified stake would reduce the principal governance objection; repeated roadmap deferral would make the permissioned model a durable feature rather than a transition.

watch.signal: TVL, stablecoins, DEX volume, fees, and retained revenue tracked separately from raw transaction counts.
watch.implication: Growth in independent economic measures would support durable demand; high operator-reported throughput without revenue would not.

watch.signal: Security incidents at the boundary between native services, precompiles, and EVM applications.
watch.implication: A quiet operating record and broader audit coverage would support the hybrid-service design; another boundary failure would increase integration-risk weight.

unknowns.question: When, under what admission rules, and with what stake distribution will non-Council consensus nodes be allowed?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A deployed permissionless-node release with an auditable operator set.

unknowns.question: How concentrated is fee-paying demand by application or enterprise customer?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: An independent entity-level fee and transaction decomposition.

unknowns.question: What portion of current activity is subsidized by ecosystem grants or treasury allocations?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Reconciled grant flows matched to application-level usage and fees.

unknowns.question: How much undistributed or restricted HBAR is controlled by Council-linked or ecosystem entities?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A current audited treasury and restriction schedule.

observation_snapshot.method: One sequential client run: stablecoinchains once, then the latest historicalChainTvl point and provider-reported 24-hour and 30-day fee, revenue, and DEX aggregates for each chain. Currency aggregates were rounded to cents. Same-day historical points can be revised after this retrieval window.

outcome.label: successful
outcome.summary: Gnosis is a successful specialist chain for inexpensive, stable-value EVM settlement, although it is not a leading general-purpose liquidity venue. In the DefiLlama snapshot begun at 2026-08-03T17:23:37.879Z, the latest 2026-08-03 point was $96.6 million TVL, 66.9% below the December 2024 peak, with $150.1 million of 30-day DEX volume, $436,346 of fees, and $24,099 of retained revenue. Its multi-currency stablecoin supply and continuing activity support a durable niche, while the June 2026 Gnosis Pay module exploit and precautionary canonical-bridge pause expose application and bridge-governance dependencies. These figures are a point-in-time snapshot.

why.summary: Observed: Gnosis retains more capital and DEX activity than many specialist chains, but TVL is below peak and protocol revenue remains modest. Documented design: xDai made stable-value gas a first-class user experience; the Gnosis merger aligned the chain with GNO staking; the 2022 Merge replaced a small authority set with Ethereum-derived proof of stake; and bridge governors retained explicit cross-chain controls. The chain later used an encrypted mempool as a live neutrality experiment. Strategic inference: compatibility with Ethereum clients, cheap stable gas, a large validator set, and payment-oriented products created a durable settlement niche without requiring Gnosis to win the base-asset or rollup race. The trade-off is layered trust: validators, bridge governors, stablecoin issuers, application modules, and Shutter keypers secure different boundaries. The 2026 card-safe exploit was not a consensus failure, but the bridge pause shows how an application incident can activate chain-adjacent control.

strategic_choices.decision: Keep xDai as the native gas asset while using GNO for proof-of-stake security.
strategic_choices.consequence: Users receive predictable stable-value gas and stakers retain a separate security asset, but value capture and issuer dependencies are split across tokens.

strategic_choices.decision: Merge xDai and Gnosis governance, then replace the authority model with Ethereum-style proof of stake.
strategic_choices.consequence: The chain gained a much larger validator set and shared client architecture while accepting the operational complexity of a full beacon chain.

strategic_choices.decision: Govern canonical bridges through named governors and validators while adding light-client and multi-oracle paths.
strategic_choices.consequence: The network can pause and harden cross-chain flows, but bridge security and emergency power remain distinct from base consensus.

strategic_choices.decision: Deploy threshold-encrypted transaction submission through Shutter.
strategic_choices.consequence: Users can reduce public-mempool front-running, while liveness and correct decryption add a separate keyper and validator coordination layer.

counterfactual.summary: Remaining a small authority-operated xDai chain would have been simpler and potentially easier to coordinate, but would preserve a clear centralization ceiling. Becoming an Ethereum rollup could inherit stronger settlement and bridge conventions, but would trade sovereign validator participation for sequencer and rollup dependencies. Removing bridge pause powers might improve credible-neutrality optics while limiting containment during application incidents. The available evidence supports these trade-offs but does not prove which architecture would have produced more payments, TVL, or revenue.

watch.signal: TVL, multi-currency stablecoin supply, DEX volume, fees, and retained revenue.
watch.implication: Broad growth would show the payments niche deepening into a larger economy; volume without revenue would keep value capture limited.

watch.signal: Bridge-validator composition, light-client adoption, pause decisions, and recovery times.
watch.implication: More independently verified paths would reduce trusted-bridge exposure; repeated emergency pauses would show control remains a central safety mechanism.

watch.signal: Encrypted-mempool participation, keyper diversity, failed decryptions, and fallback behavior.
watch.implication: Reliable adoption would support Gnosis as a credible-neutrality test bed; thin use or liveness failures would make Shutter an optional niche feature.

unknowns.question: What share of current Gnosis activity comes from payments versus trading, incentives, bots, or internal treasury flows?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: An independent application- and entity-level fee decomposition.

unknowns.question: How concentrated are GNO stake, validator operators, and client implementations?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A current validator, entity, and client-diversity audit.

unknowns.question: What value is exposed to each bridge-validator path and emergency governor set?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A current bridge-by-bridge value and signer map.

unknowns.question: How many transactions use the encrypted mempool and how often does it fall back to public submission?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Public longitudinal Shutter usage and liveness telemetry.

observation_snapshot.method: One sequential client run: stablecoinchains once, then the latest historicalChainTvl point and provider-reported 24-hour and 30-day fee, revenue, and DEX aggregates for each chain. Currency aggregates were rounded to cents. Same-day historical points can be revised after this retrieval window.

outcome.label: declining
outcome.summary: Osmosis is a declining but still operating exchange appchain. In the DefiLlama snapshot begun at 2026-08-03T17:23:37.879Z, the latest 2026-08-03 point was $12.3 million TVL, 99.3% below the March 2022 peak, alongside $28.3 million of dollar stablecoins, $45.2 million of 30-day DEX volume, $29,934 of fees, and $11,431 of retained revenue. Continued routing and trading show that the product has not disappeared, but capital retention and security-budget economics are far below the incentive-era peak. The 2022 pool-accounting exploit and validator halt remain material evidence about application-chain emergency coordination. These figures are a point-in-time snapshot.

why.summary: Observed: Osmosis still clears trades and retains stablecoin liquidity, but TVL is more than ninety-nine percent below peak and current fees and revenue are small. Documented design: it launched as a sovereign Cosmos exchange chain so governance could control pools, routing, incentives, fee logic, upgrades, and IBC integrations at the protocol level. Strategic inference: specialization and IBC made Osmosis a natural venue for fragmented Cosmos assets, while OSMO emissions accelerated liquidity formation. Those choices did not make liquidity permanent: incentive sensitivity, the Terra ecosystem shock, fragmented interchain demand, and an independent validator security budget all pressure retention. The 2022 exploit provides direct evidence that a pool-accounting defect could become chain-wide and that validators could coordinate a halt; it does not by itself prove the later drawdown, which must remain an unattributed observed outcome rather than a single-cause story.

strategic_choices.decision: Build a sovereign appchain around exchange execution rather than deploy an AMM on a shared chain.
strategic_choices.consequence: Governance can control routing, fees, upgrades, and market primitives, while the protocol must maintain its own validator security and operational stack.

strategic_choices.decision: Use IBC as the primary asset-distribution and interoperability rail.
strategic_choices.consequence: Many Cosmos assets can reach a common venue, but relayer outages, connected-zone failures, and ecosystem fragmentation become demand and safety dependencies.

strategic_choices.decision: Use OSMO governance and incentives to bootstrap and direct liquidity.
strategic_choices.consequence: Pools can form quickly and community governance can target emissions, but mercenary capital can leave when rewards or token prices weaken.

strategic_choices.decision: Coordinate a validator halt after the 2022 pool-share accounting exploit.
strategic_choices.consequence: The network limited further loss and enabled recovery, while demonstrating that validator coordination and application logic are part of the same systemic boundary.

counterfactual.summary: Launching as contracts on a larger shared chain could have reduced the independent security and validator burden and placed Osmosis closer to a deeper base of collateral, but would sacrifice protocol-level control over exchange execution and IBC-native routing. Using fewer incentives might have produced a smaller, more organic initial liquidity base, but could also have prevented Osmosis from becoming a Cosmos hub. The reviewed evidence cannot establish that either alternative would have survived Terra contagion better or retained more long-run volume.

watch.signal: TVL, stablecoin supply, DEX volume, fees, and retained revenue, with incentive spending reported separately.
watch.implication: Revenue and capital growth without higher subsidies would support a recovery; volume that depends on emissions would leave the retention problem intact.

watch.signal: Validator voting-power concentration, security budget, and emergency-halt participation.
watch.implication: A diverse set with adequate economics reduces coordinated-failure risk; concentration or falling rewards would weaken sovereign-chain resilience.

watch.signal: IBC route diversity, relayer concentration, and share of volume tied to a few connected zones.
watch.implication: Broader routes would make the hub less dependent on any one ecosystem; concentration would preserve contagion risk.

unknowns.question: What share of current volume and TVL is directly or indirectly incentive-dependent?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A pool-level subsidy, liquidity, and organic-volume decomposition.

unknowns.question: How concentrated are validator voting power, hosting, and governance participation?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A current independent entity-level validator map.

unknowns.question: Which IBC routes and relayers carry most economic value and how often do they fail?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Longitudinal route-level value, relayer, and outage telemetry.

unknowns.question: Which applications and pools generate current protocol revenue, and how much accrues to OSMO holders or the community pool?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A reconciled fee-flow and value-accrual statement.

outcome.label: middling
outcome.summary: Stacks is a technically distinct but middling Bitcoin-linked smart-contract network. In the DefiLlama snapshot begun at 2026-08-03T17:23:37.879Z, the latest 2026-08-03 point was $75.9 million TVL, 60.9% below the April 2024 peak, alongside $12.3 million of dollar stablecoins, $21.4 million of 30-day DEX volume, $74,756 of fees, and $16,403 of retained revenue. Nakamoto block production and sBTC make the Bitcoin application thesis more usable, but current independent activity remains modest and the July 2025 stall shows that signer and node upgrade coordination can interrupt liveness. These figures are a point-in-time snapshot.

why.summary: Observed: Stacks retains meaningful TVL but modest stablecoin, DEX, fee, and revenue activity relative to larger smart-contract ecosystems. Documented design: proof of transfer anchors miner selection and settlement to Bitcoin; Nakamoto allows multiple faster Stacks blocks during a Bitcoin tenure and adds signer validation; Clarity makes contract behavior deliberately explicit; and sBTC uses a threshold signer set to move BTC into programmable applications. Strategic inference: the architecture can offer Bitcoin-linked finality and BTC-denominated collateral without changing Bitcoin itself, which differentiates Stacks from generic EVM execution. The cost is a layered dependency on Bitcoin blocks, miners, stackers/signers, node software, and the sBTC wallet. The July 2025 stall, caused by outdated large signers encountering a known reorg-related bug, directly demonstrates coordination and upgrade risk. It does not prove the Bitcoin-layer strategy caused weak adoption, so current metrics remain outcome evidence rather than causal proof.

strategic_choices.decision: Use proof of transfer and Bitcoin anchoring instead of launching an independent proof-of-stake security system.
strategic_choices.consequence: Stacks reuses Bitcoin blocks and BTC commitments for ordering and settlement context, while retaining its own miners, signers, execution, and liveness risks.

strategic_choices.decision: Adopt Nakamoto block production with signer-approved blocks inside each Bitcoin tenure.
strategic_choices.consequence: Transactions can confirm faster and gain stronger reorg resistance, but signer participation and timely node upgrades become critical liveness dependencies.

strategic_choices.decision: Use Clarity and a distinct execution environment rather than EVM compatibility.
strategic_choices.consequence: Developers gain decidable contracts and Bitcoin-aware primitives, while portability, tooling, and liquidity composition are narrower than in EVM ecosystems.

strategic_choices.decision: Bridge BTC through sBTC threshold signers selected for an initial staged rollout.
strategic_choices.consequence: BTC becomes programmable without a centralized custodian, but custody and withdrawal liveness depend on a bounded signer set whose decentralization is still evolving.

counterfactual.summary: Building as an EVM sidechain or rollup could have imported more tooling and liquidity, but would weaken Stacks' differentiated Clarity and proof-of-transfer design and still require a BTC bridge. Waiting for a fully open sBTC signer set before launch could reduce concentration concerns, while delaying the collateral primitive needed to test Bitcoin DeFi. Keeping pre-Nakamoto block production would avoid new signer complexity but retain slow confirmation and congestion. The evidence identifies these trade-offs without proving an alternative would have delivered more usage or perfect liveness.

watch.signal: TVL, sBTC supply, stablecoins, DEX volume, fees, and retained revenue tracked separately.
watch.implication: Growth in BTC collateral and recurring revenue would validate more of the Bitcoin-application thesis; TVL without usage would leave capital efficiency unresolved.

watch.signal: Signer-set size, entity diversity, software-version adoption, missed signatures, and stalls.
watch.implication: Broad, current participation would reduce liveness concentration; repeated failures among a few large signers would make coordination the binding risk.

watch.signal: sBTC deposit and withdrawal caps, completion times, signer rotations, and failed requests.
watch.implication: Reliable two-way conversion under rising balances supports the bridge design; delayed withdrawals or concentrated signers increase custody-risk weight.

unknowns.question: How concentrated are Stacks miners, Nakamoto signers, and the infrastructure they operate?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A current independent entity-level mining, signer, and hosting map.

unknowns.question: What share of TVL is sBTC and how concentrated is it by protocol and depositor?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A reproducible asset- and holder-level TVL decomposition.

unknowns.question: How often do signer disagreement, outdated software, or Bitcoin reorg handling delay blocks?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: Public longitudinal signer and liveness telemetry.

unknowns.question: How do gross fees, miner rewards, signer rewards, and STX value accrual reconcile?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A complete independently reproducible fee and reward-flow statement.
